Tentative Rulings
February 27, 2026
Department S-17
Judge Joseph Ortiz
______________________________________________________________________
Tentative Rulings for Department S-17 are posted on the court’s website (https://www.sb-
court.org/divisions/civil/civil-tentative-rulings) at 3:00 p.m. or at 7:00 p.m. the court day before
the hearing. If no tentative ruling is posted at 3:00 p.m., please check again after 7:00 p.m.
Unless you wish to submit on the tentative ruling, you must appear for the hearing either in
person, CourtCall (888-882-6878 or www.courtcall.com), or by ZOOM. Failure to appear is
deemed a waiver of oral argument. If you wish to submit to the tentative, please call the
Judicial Assistant at (909) 708-8715 in advance of the hearing. If all parties submit on a
tentative ruling, it will become final. The tentative ruling may seek input on particular issues
and direct appearance. If so directed, attendance at the hearing is mandatory. The party
prevailing on a motion or other hearing shall serve written notice of the court’s ruling unless all
parties waive notice of the ruling.
ATTENTION: As of January 9, 2023, the court no longer provides an official Court Reporter to
transcribe proceedings. Parties who wish to have a transcript must retain their own private
reporter and must submit a “Stipulation and Order to Use Certified Shorthand Reporter.”
Parties who do not retain their own reporter have waived the right to one.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF THE RULING.
1
13. Pacific Allied Group, Inc., v. Medina, Case No. CIVSB2415189
Motion to be Relieved as Counsel for Plaintiff
2/27/26, 9:00 a.m., S-17
The Court would GRANT this unopposed motion, filed by Jeffrey Kenny, Esq. and Kenny Law
Group P.C., relating to representation of Plaintiff Pacific Allied. The motion is supported by a
declaration establishing good cause and the breakdown of the attorney-client relationship.
(Kenny Decl.) The Court would also order the at-issue Plaintiff to have a representative appear
before the Court at an OSC regarding representation. As a corporation, Plaintiff may not
represent itself. Plaintiff is to inform the Court on the status of their representation and
prosecution of the case.
The relief is not effective until service of the ruling has been effectuated and proof of service
has been filed.
*** *** ***
14. Strege, et al, v. Ford Motor Company, et al, Case No. CIVSB2437208
Plaintiffs’ Motion to Compel Further Responses to Requests for Production, Set One
Plaintiffs’ Motion to Compel Further Responses to Special Interrogatories, Set One
2/27/26, 9:00 a.m., S-17
Tentative Ruling
The Court would GRANT these two unopposed motions. As to the Requests for Production,
further responses are due to numbers 16-24, 30, 37, 39, 41, 49, 50-51, 79, 81, 83, 85, 87, 89, 91,
93, and 96-97. As to the Special Interrogatories, further responses are due to numbers 6, 15-17,
27-28, and 99-102. Supplemental responses are due within thirty days.
The Court would further GRANT sanctions in the amount of $2,500. Sanctions are also due
within thirty days.
Case Summary
This is a lemon law case. On or about February 23, 2019, Plaintiffs purchased the subject
vehicle. They assert that the vehicle included warranties. However, they assert that there were
transmission defects and nonconformities within the warranty period. They assert that
Defendant knew or should have known of the defects and should not have sold the vehicle.
They further allege that Defendant concealed its knowledge of the defects. Notwithstanding,
they also alleged they are entitled to replacement or restitution, and that, despite adequate
opportunity, Defendant has failed to provide replacement or restitution. As such, they filed suit
on December 17, 2024, asserting causes of action for: (1) Breach of Express Warranty (Song-
2
Beverly Act (Act)); (2) Violation of Section 1793.2 (Act); (3) fraudulent inducement –
concealment; and (4) negligent repair.
Relevant here, Plaintiff sent its first sets of discovery on April 24, 2025, including the at-issue
Requests for Production, Set One (RFP1) and Special Interrogatories, Set One (SROG1). (Meagle
Decl., ¶3 & Exh. A.)1 Defendant responses on May 27, 2025, with verifications following.
(Meagle Decl., ¶4.) Plaintiff thereafter sent a meet-and-confer letter. (Id., ¶5 & Exh. C.) Further
attempts at meet-and-conferring followed, including additional letters as well as a stipulated
continuance for the purpose of addressing discovery concerns.
Analysis
As a preliminary matter, the Court notes that the parties stipulated on December 11, 2025, to
continue these motions to this date. That stipulation expressed a belief that meet-and-confer
efforts would moot these instant motions. The order continuing the hearings to this date was
signed on December 17, 2025. Since that date, movant has not requested the withdrawal of the
motions nor has Defendant opposed either motion. However, the Court is cognizant that failure
to withdraw the motions may be an oversight.
Nonetheless, as the matters have not been withdrawn, the Court notes that there is no
opposition and the arguments are, therefore, conceded. (DuPont Merck Pharmaceutical Co. v.
Superior Court (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 562, 566 [“By failing to argue the contrary, plaintiffs
concede this issue.”]; see Pacifica First National, Inc. v. Abekasis (2021) 50 Cal.App.5th 654, 657
[Not returning to a topic on reply, “is a concession.”].) The Court would, therefore, grant the
motions.
*** *** ***
17. Franklin v. National Community Renaissance, Case No. CIVSB2209612
Motion for Approval of PAGA Representative Action Settlement
2/27/26, 1:30 p.m., Dept. S-17
This matter was continued from February 2, 2026
Tentative Ruling
The Court would GRANT presuming attorneys’ fees are lowered to 1/3rd of the gross, or
$330,000.00, as discussed infra. (See FN 3.)
1 While separate declarations are submitted for each motion, they are largely identical. Thus, the same paragraph
and exhibit identification are applicable to each motion.
3
Standards
Settlements under the Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA) at Labor Code sections 2698, et
seq., do not require preliminary approval. The court must find, however, that the PAGA
settlement is “fair, reasonable, and adequate in view of PAGA’s purposes to remediate present
labor law violations, deter future ones, and to maximize enforcement of state labor laws.”
(Moniz v. Adecco USA, Inc. (2021) 72 Cal.App.5th 56, 77.) The court must find that the plaintiff
“has adequately represented the state’s interests, and hence the public interest.” (Id. at p. 89.)
The LWDA must be notified of the settlement and be given an opportunity to object.
The Court may looks to parallel class action guidelines to determine what is “fair, adequate and
reasonable.” (Kullar v. Foot Locker Retail (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 116, 126.) In that analysis, the
court has “broad discretion in making this determination.” (In re Microsoft I-V Cases (2006) 135
Cal.App.4th 706, 723.) Relevant factors may include “the strength of the plaintiffs’ case, the
risk, expense, complexity and likely duration of further litigation, the risk of maintain class
action status through trial, the amount offered in settlement, the extent of discovery
completed and the stage of the proceedings, the experience and views of counsel, the presence
of a governmental participant, and the reaction of the class members to the proposed
settlement.” (Dunk v. Ford Motor Co. (1996) 48 Cal.App.4th 1794, 1801.) This list of factors “is
not exhaustive and should be tailored to each case.” (Ibid.) The court may “engage in a
balancing and weighing of factors depending on the circumstances of each case.” (Wershba v.
Apple Computer, Inc. (2001) 91 Cal.App.4th 224, 245 [overruled on other grounds].)
“Although the court gives regard to what is otherwise a private consensual agreement between
the parties, the court must also evaluate the proposed settlement agreement with the purpose
of protecting the rights of the absent class members who will be bound by the settlement.”
(Wershba, supra, 91 Cal.App.4th at p. 245, quoting Dunk, supra, 48 Cal.App.4th at p. 1801.)
“The court must therefore scrutinize the proposed settlement agreement to the extent
necessary to ‘reach a reasoned judgment that the agreement is not the product of fraud or
overreaching by, or collusion between, the negotiating parties, and that the settlement, taken
as a whole, is fair, reasonable and adequate to all concerned.’” (Ibid., quoting Officers for
Justice v. Civil Service Com’n (9th Cir. 1982) 688 F.2d 615, 625.)
The settlement is entitled to “a presumption of fairness . . . where: (1) the settlement is
reached through arm’s-length bargaining; (2) investigation and discovery are sufficient to allow
counsel and the court to act intelligently; (3) counsel is experienced in similar litigation; and (4)
the percentage of objectors is small.” (Kullar v. Foot Locker Retail (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 116,
128, quoting Dunk v. Ford Motor Co. (1996) 48 Cal.App.4th 1794, 1802.)
In this case, the Court finds the proposed PAGA settlement to fair, reasonable, and adequate.
The amount of the settlement appears to be appropriate given the strength of plaintiff’s case
and the risks involved in litigation. Adequate discovery and investigation has occurred. There is
no evidence of fraud or collusion, and class counsel are well-qualified to represent the class.
The Court is unaware of any disqualifying features for the class representative.
4
The Proposed Settlement
Here, on March 3, 2022, Plaintiff originally submitted his notice letter to the Labor and
Workforce Development Agency (LWDA) to setting forth various allegations of wage-and-hour
violations. Shortly thereafter, after the exhaustion of administrative remedies, he filed this
instant suit on May 10, 2022. The Complaint set forth a single cause of action for civil penalties
pursuant to the Private Attorneys General Act (PAGA), underpinned by various purported wage-
and-hour violations, including those relating to overtime, meal periods, rest breaks, minimum
wages, final pay, wage timeliness, accurate wage statements, accurate payroll records, and
reimbursements.
After commencing the initial litigation, the parties conducted significant investigation of the
facts and law and engaged in an informal discovery exchange prior to mediation, including time
and payroll data. (Sweeny Supp. Decl., ¶9.) Thereafter, the parties attended a full-day, arms-
length mediation on March 6, 2025, with Hon. Peter Wilson (Ret.), an experienced neutral.
(Settlement, ¶1(c).) While the case did not settle immediately, the parties ultimately reached a
settlement in the abstract. A long-form settlement agreement was reached by November of
2025. The LWDA was provided notice on December 10, 2025. (See Sweeny 2nd. Supp. Decl.,
¶18.)
The settlement covers all nonexempt employed by Defendant in California who worked at least
one pay period for Defendant any time between March 11, 2019,2 and March 5, 2025.
(Settlement, ¶3(a)(5).) Further, the parties indicate that there are approximately 900 such
aggrieved employees. (Sweeny 2nd. Supp. Decl., ¶10.)
The settlement proposed the following terms: Defendant will pay a gross settlement amount of
$990,000.00, from which will be deducted (1) attorneys’ fees of 346,500.00 (35% the gross);3
(2) costs no more than $25,000.00; (3) Plaintiff’s enhancement fee of no more than $7,500.00
and (3) claims administration fees of no more than $25,000.00.
Presuming 1/3rd the gross for attorneys’ fees, the net settlement would be $602,500.00.
Of that amount, 75%, or $451,875.00, would go to the LWDA, and 25%, or $150,625.00, would
go to the aggrieved employees on a pro rata basis determined by the number of applicable pay
periods worked. Notably, given the 900 aggrieved employees, the average PAGA payout to the
employees would be $167.36.
2 The Court sought further input as to why it is appropriate to extend the PAGA period beyond that available
pursuant to the Statute of Limitations. Rather than provide factual input regarding negotiation and consideration,
counsel simply reiterated the law. (Sweeny 2nd Supp. Decl., ¶¶12-13.) The Court is already apprised of the law.
However, the Court is inclined to view the statements as implying discussion and negotiation regarding the
extended period. Counsel is admonished to provide better detail of the facts in the future.
3 The Court will approve 1/3rd the gross, or $330,000.00, which still represents a significant multiplier – sufficient
to reward the risk and complexity of this matter - on the lodestar. (See Sweeny Decl., ¶19 & Exh. 2 [130.2 hrs].)
Counsel may make further argument at hearing why the requested 35% is more appropriate.
5
The amount of the settlement is appropriate given the purported exposure and, importantly,
the strength of plaintiff’s case. There has been adequate discovery and investigation. There is
no evidence of fraud or collusion. The settlement was reached through an arms-length
negotiation with the assistance of an experienced mediator.
*** *** ***
